title: Concepts of Quantum Mechanics
short_intro: Quantum mechanics provides the fundamental framework for describing physical systems at atomic and subatomic scales where classical mechanics fails. It introduces wave-particle duality, operator algebra, and probabilistic interpretation of physical observables.

exam_scope.tgt_core: Basic postulates of wave-particle duality, de Broglie wavelength, Heisenberg's Uncertainty Principle, and elementary properties of wave functions.
exam_scope.pgt_extension: Time-dependent and time-independent Schrödinger wave equations, expectation values, Hermitian operators, normalization conditions, and probability current density.

concept_notes.heading: Wave-Particle Duality and de Broglie Hypothesis
bullets: All material particles in motion possess an associated wave nature with wavelength inversely proportional to linear momentum.
The de Broglie wavelength is expressed as \lambda = h / p, where h is Planck's constant.
This duality bridges corpuscular and undulatory descriptions, forming the foundation of matter waves.

concept_notes.heading: Heisenberg's Uncertainty Principle
bullets: It is fundamentally impossible to simultaneously measure certain pairs of conjugate variables, such as position and momentum, with arbitrary precision.
The minimum uncertainty product is given by \Delta x \Delta p_x \ge \frac{\hbar}{2}.
Energy and time also satisfy an uncertainty relation \Delta E \Delta t \ge \frac{\hbar}{2}, explaining natural line broadening.

concept_notes.heading: Schrödinger Wave Equation and Wave Function
bullets: The state of a quantum system is completely specified by a wave function \Psi(r, t), which contains all accessible physical information.
Max Born's statistical interpretation states that the absolute square |\Psi|^2 represents the probability density of finding a particle at a given point.
The time-independent Schrödinger equation governs stationary states of a quantum system under a time-independent potential.

concept_notes.heading: Operators and Expectation Values
bullets: Every observable in quantum mechanics is represented by a linear, Hermitian operator acting on the wave function.
Eigenvalues of an operator correspond to the measurable values of the physical observable.
The expectation value \langle A \rangle represents the statistical average outcome of numerous measurements performed on identically prepared systems.

derivations.title: Time-Independent Schrödinger Equation
derivations.conditions: Conservative system with time-independent potential energy V(r)
steps: Start with the general wave function separation of variables: \Psi(r, t) = \psi(r) e^{-i \frac{E}{\hbar} t}.
Substitute \Psi(r, t) into the time-dependent Schrödinger equation: - \frac{\hbar^2}{2m} \nabla^2 \Psi + V \Psi = i \hbar \frac{\partial \Psi}{\partial t}.
Evaluate the time derivative yielding E \psi(r) e^{-i \frac{E}{\hbar} t} on the right-hand side.
Divide both sides by the exponential term e^{-i \frac{E}{\hbar} t} to obtain the time-independent equation.

derivations.title: de Broglie Wavelength of an Accelerated Electron
derivations.conditions: Non-relativistic electron accelerated from rest through potential difference V
steps: Equate the kinetic energy gained to electrical potential energy: \frac{1}{2} mv^2 = eV.
Express momentum p in terms of kinetic energy: p = mv = \sqrt{2mE} = \sqrt{2meV}.
Substitute momentum into the de Broglie relation \lambda = \frac{h}{p}.
Substitute standard values of h, m, and e to obtain the working formula in terms of V.

graphs_and_experiments.title: Davisson-Germer Experiment Setup
graphs_and_experiments.what_to_draw: Electron gun, nickel crystal target, and movable Faraday cylinder detector showing scattered intensity vs. scattering angle \theta at various accelerating voltages.
graphs_and_experiments.interpretation: A sharp peak in electron scattering intensity at \theta = 50^\circ and V = 54\text{ V} confirms electron wave interference (Bragg's law), proving de Broglie's wave hypothesis.
graphs_and_experiments.exam_use: Direct questions on accelerating potential, scattering angle, and experimental proof of matter waves.

graphs_and_experiments.title: Probability Density Distribution |\psi_n(x)|^2 for Particle in a Box
graphs_and_experiments.what_to_draw: Sine-squared curves representing probability density inside a 1D infinite potential well for n = 1, 2, 3.
graphs_and_experiments.interpretation: Shows spatial regions where the particle is most likely (antinodes) and least likely (nodes) to be found, contrasting sharply with classical uniform probability.
graphs_and_experiments.exam_use: Interpreting quantum states, node counting, and finding high-probability regions.

graphs_and_experiments.title: Potential Step Reflection and Transmission
graphs_and_experiments.what_to_draw: Incident, reflected, and transmitted wave amplitudes across a potential step of height V_0 where E < V_0.
graphs_and_experiments.interpretation: Demonstrates quantum tunneling where the wave function penetrates classically forbidden regions with an exponential decay envelope.
graphs_and_experiments.exam_use: Understanding penetration depth and reflection coefficients.

solved_numericals.question: Calculate the de Broglie wavelength of a proton accelerated through a potential difference of 100 V. (Mass of proton = 1.67 \times 10^{-27} kg, h = 6.63 \times 10^{-34} J s)
solution_steps: Substitute values: h = 6.63 \times 10^{-34}, m = 1.67 \times 10^{-27}, e = 1.6 \times 10^{-19}, V = 100.

solved_numericals.question: A particle of mass m is moving in a 1D infinite potential well of width L. If its wave function is given by \psi(x) = \sqrt{\frac{2}{L}} \sin\left(\frac{\pi x}{L}\right) for 0 \le x \le L, find its expectation value of position \langle x \rangle.
solution_steps: Set up the expectation integral: \langle x \rangle = \int_{0}^{L} \psi^*(x) x \psi(x) \, dx.
Substitute wave function: \langle x \rangle = \frac{2}{L} \int_{0}^{L} x \sin^2\left(\frac{\pi x}{L}\right) dx.
Use trigonometric identity \sin^2\theta = \frac{1 - \cos(2\theta)}{2}: \langle x \rangle = \frac{2}{L} \int_{0}^{L} x \left[ \frac{1 - \cos(\frac{2\pi x}{L})}{2} \right] dx.
Integrate term by term: \frac{1}{L} \left[ \frac{x^2}{2} \right]_0^L - \frac{1}{L} \int_{0}^{L} x \cos\left(\frac{2\pi x}{L}\right) dx.
The integral of x \cos(kx) over a full period evaluates to zero by symmetry.

solved_numericals.question: An electron is confined to a region of size 1 \text{ \AA}. Estimate the minimum uncertainty in its velocity.
solution_steps: Apply Heisenberg uncertainty principle for momentum: \Delta p_x \ge \frac{\hbar}{2 \Delta x}.
Substitute \hbar = 1.054 \times 10^{-34} \text{ J s}: \Delta p_x = \frac{1.054 \times 10^{-34}}{2 \times 10^{-10}} = 5.27 \times 10^{-25} \text{ kg m s^{-1}}.
Relate momentum uncertainty to velocity uncertainty: \Delta v_x = \frac{\Delta p_x}{m}.

Substitute electron mass m = 9.1 \times 10^{-31} \text{ kg}: \Delta v_x = \frac{5.27 \times 10^{-25}}{9.1 \times 10^{-10}} \text{ (wait, mass is 9.1e-31)} \Rightarrow \frac{5.27 \times 10^{-25}}{9.1 \times 10^{-31}} = 5.79 \times 10^5 \text{ m s^{-1}}.

assumptions_and_limitations: Non-relativistic quantum mechanics assumes particle velocities are much smaller than the speed of light, failing for high-energy subatomic processes requiring Dirac's relativistic wave equation.
Potential functions V(r) are treated as externally prescribed classical fields, ignoring back-reaction of the quantum particle on the field in elementary formulations.

common_misconceptions.wrong: The wave function \Psi itself is a physical wave propagating in space like a sound or light wave.
common_misconceptions.correct: The wave function is a mathematical probability amplitude whose square modulus represents probability density.
common_misconceptions.why: \Psi can take complex values and does not transport physical energy or mass directly.

common_misconceptions.wrong: Heisenberg's Uncertainty Principle is caused by mechanical disturbance of the instrument during measurement.
common_misconceptions.correct: It is an inherent intrinsic property of quantum states arising from the non-commuting nature of operators.
common_misconceptions.why: Even with infinitely sensitive, hypothetical disturbance-free instruments, the fundamental wave packet spread persists.

quick_revision: Matter waves have wavelength \lambda = h / p, verified by Davisson and Germer.
Stationary states satisfy the time-independent Schrödinger equation H\psi = E\psi.
The wave function must be single-valued, continuous, and normalizable.
